# Introduction

This report presents a machine learning analysis to predict diabetes outcomes using the **Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset**. The analysis covers data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, model training, and evaluation.

---

# Load Packages

```{r packages}
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(ggplot2)
library(corrplot)
library(dplyr)
```

---

# Step 1: Import Dataset {.tabset}

```{r import}
diabetes <- read.csv("data/diabetes.csv", header = FALSE)

names(diabetes) <- c(
  "Pregnancies", "Glucose", "BloodPressure",
  "SkinThickness", "Insulin", "BMI",
  "DiabetesPedigreeFunction", "Age", "Outcome"
)

cat("Dataset Dimensions:", dim(diabetes), "\n")
```

## First 6 Rows

```{r head}
head(diabetes)
```

## Structure

```{r str}
str(diabetes)
```

## Summary Statistics

```{r summary}
summary(diabetes)
```

---

# Step 2: Data Cleaning & Preprocessing

## Missing Values (Before)

```{r missing-before}
colSums(is.na(diabetes))
```

## Invalid Zero Values

Columns where **zero is medically invalid**:

```{r zeros}
invalid_cols <- c("Glucose", "BloodPressure", "SkinThickness", "Insulin", "BMI")
colSums(diabetes[, invalid_cols] == 0)
```

## Median Imputation

```{r impute}
# Replace zeros with NA
for (col in invalid_cols) {
  diabetes[diabetes[[col]] == 0, col] <- NA
}

# Replace NA with column median
for (col in invalid_cols) {
  med <- median(diabetes[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  diabetes[[col]][is.na(diabetes[[col]])] <- med
}

# Verify
cat("Missing values after imputation:\n")
colSums(is.na(diabetes))
```

```{r factor}
diabetes$Outcome <- factor(diabetes$Outcome, levels = c(0, 1),
                           labels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

---

# Step 3: Exploratory Data Analysis

## Outcome Distribution

```{r outcome-dist}
outcome_tbl <- as.data.frame(table(diabetes$Outcome))
names(outcome_tbl) <- c("Outcome", "Count")
outcome_tbl$Percent <- round(prop.table(outcome_tbl$Count) * 100, 1)
outcome_tbl
```

## Group Means by Outcome

```{r group-means}
num_cols <- names(diabetes)[sapply(diabetes, is.numeric)]

diabetes %>%
  group_by(Outcome) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(num_cols), mean, .names = "mean_{.col}"))
```

# Step 4: Visualizations {.tabset}

## Outcome Distribution

```{r plot-outcome}
ggplot(diabetes, aes(x = Outcome, fill = Outcome)) +
```

## Correlation Heatmap

```{r plot-corr, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
cor_mat <- cor(diabetes %>% mutate(Outcome = as.numeric(Outcome)))
corrplot(cor_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45, tl.cex = 0.8, number.cex = 0.65,
         mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0),
         title = "Feature Correlation Matrix")
```

---

# Step 5: Train / Test Split

```{r split}
set.seed(42)
train_idx  <- createDataPartition(diabetes$Outcome, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_data <- diabetes[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- diabetes[-train_idx, ]

cat("Training set:", nrow(train_data), "rows\n")
cat("Testing set: ", nrow(test_data),  "rows\n")
```

---

# Step 6: Model Training

```{r cv-setup}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
                     savePredictions = TRUE)
```

## Logistic Regression

```{r model-lr}
set.seed(42)
model_lr <- train(Outcome ~ ., data = train_data,
                  method = "glm", family = "binomial",
                  trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC")

cat("CV ROC (Logistic Regression):", round(max(model_lr$results$ROC), 4))
```

## Random Forest

```{r model-rf}
set.seed(42)
model_rf <- train(Outcome ~ ., data = train_data,
                  method = "rf",
                  trControl = ctrl, metric = "ROC",
                  tuneLength = 3)

cat("CV ROC (Random Forest):", round(max(model_rf$results$ROC), 4))
```

---

# Step 7: Model Evaluation {.tabset}

```{r eval-fn, echo=FALSE}
eval_table <- function(model, test_data) {
  preds <- predict(model, test_data)
  cm    <- confusionMatrix(preds, test_data$Outcome, positive = "Yes")
  data.frame(
    Metric = c("Accuracy", "Sensitivity (Recall)",
               "Specificity", "Precision", "F1 Score"),
    Value  = round(c(
      cm$overall["Accuracy"],
      cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
      cm$byClass["Specificity"],
      cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
      cm$byClass["F1"]
    ), 4)
  )
}
```

## Logistic Regression

```{r eval-lr}
preds_lr <- predict(model_lr, test_data)
cm_lr    <- confusionMatrix(preds_lr, test_data$Outcome, positive = "Yes")
print(cm_lr$table)
eval_table(model_lr, test_data)
```

## Random Forest

```{r eval-rf}
preds_rf <- predict(model_rf, test_data)
cm_rf    <- confusionMatrix(preds_rf, test_data$Outcome, positive = "Yes")
print(cm_rf$table)
eval_table(model_rf, test_data)
```

---

# Step 8: Feature Importance

```{r feature-imp, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
importance_df           <- varImp(model_rf)$importance
importance_df$Feature   <- rownames(importance_df)
colnames(importance_df)[1] <- "Importance"
importance_df <- importance_df[order(-importance_df$Importance), ]

ggplot(importance_df,
       aes(x = reorder(Feature, Importance), y = Importance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Feature Importance — Random Forest",
       x = "Feature", y = "Importance (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

# Step 9: Model Comparison Summary

```{r comparison}
acc_lr <- cm_lr$overall["Accuracy"]
acc_rf <- cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"]

comparison <- data.frame(
  Model      = c("Logistic Regression", "Random Forest"),
  CV_ROC     = c(round(max(model_lr$results$ROC), 4),
                 round(max(model_rf$results$ROC), 4)),
  Test_Acc   = c(round(acc_lr, 4), round(acc_rf, 4))
)

comparison
```

```{r best}
best_model <- ifelse(acc_lr >= acc_rf, "Logistic Regression", "Random Forest")
cat("Best Model (Test Accuracy):", best_model)
```

---

# Conclusion

This analysis demonstrated the application of machine learning to predict diabetes using the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset.

**Key Findings:**

- **Glucose** is the strongest predictor of diabetes outcome
- **BMI** and **Age** are also highly important features
- **Logistic Regression** achieved **76.5% accuracy** with **84.3% AUC-ROC**
- **Random Forest** achieved **72.6% accuracy** with **85.2% AUC-ROC**
- After median imputation, 374 invalid insulin values and 227 skin thickness values were corrected

**Best Model: Logistic Regression** (by test accuracy)

> ⚠️ *This analysis is for academic purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical diagnosis.*
